title: Using AI-assisted art in a small idle game - Clicker Kids
author: Forge450
selftext:
I am the developer of Clicker Kids, a free idle/clicker game, and the project uses AI generated artwork. I am interested in feedback from people who think about AI in game development rather than only from general players/devs.



Links:

\- Web: [https://clickerkids.fun/](https://clickerkids.fun/)

\- Steam: [https://store.steampowered.com/app/4355950/Clicker\_Kids/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4355950/Clicker_Kids/)



I want to know if:

The art direction feels overall coherent enough for a small idle/indie game

The AI art will always  create trust issues for players or if I can somehow fix that without lying about it either

  
Side note I am also curious if others have dealt with the same dismissal from players simply over the AI art used and how you deal with that kind of hate? I generally just totally ignore it, I tried to explain myself in the past budget constraints etc but it felt hopeless.  
  
Hopefully this doesnt come off as whiny but being totally honest its kind of beaten me down and taken its toll over time. Sort of thing that makes you feel like quitting, had many moments like that myself but luckily still doing it!  
  
I know the game has some level of quality because despite the AI art hate many players personally message me and leave reviews saying how much they love the game.

comments.author: Fizassist1
comments.body: Looks and feels great man! Only played for a few minutes, but yeah it all looks coherent to me.  Better than what I've made 😅.

comments.author: ponderdiggums
comments.body:
Forgive me for being honest but: This is really bad UI/UX design, and screams novice designer leaning on AI. 

The sprite art is 'fine', but I wouldn't ship this. The sprites aren't animated from what I can see, the quality of art and character design is mediocre so far, and the special FX are bland. Again, it's pretty obvious this is AI'd together. 

You say on one hand many players message you saying they love the game - what do they like about it? From the game design perspective, I don't see anything particularly novel or new here. I only tried it for a few minutes, but I couldn't tell you why I would choose your game over any of the click game competitors with more polish and support. 

On the other hand you say: "I am also curious if others have dealt with the same dismissal from players simply over the AI art used and how you deal with that kind of hate? I generally just totally ignore it, I tried to explain myself in the past budget constraints etc but it felt hopeless." I would caution new game devs to do the OPPOSITE of ignoring the feedback players give you, even if you don't like said feedback. I know you want to use AI art, it's easy and relatively frictionless these days - but your method produces output that immediately reads as slop, so players aren't even willing to look at your game. This is valuable information, do not dismiss it. 

If you haven't already, separate your game into "Features" and make a game design document manually. Write like 5 pillars that will be set in stone, these are the most important concepts that should inform all of the design in your game. Write out the controls, the win conditions and lose conditions if applicable, describe the core gameplay loop, the target audience, include some market research and how you plan to stand out from competitors, etc. Design the creatures, their backstories and how that informs their stats and gameplay, same with items and so on. Map out how the different systems interact - and THEN start building these out with AI assistance, bit by bit. This can help curb the AI slop effect. Also, for art consider an AI assisted flow with manual input - IE you feed concept sketches and descriptions into the AI, it gives you art, you touch it up and animate the parts in Aseprite or whatever you use. And seriously look into some guides for UI design and the like and move away from the AI-UI, it's generally one of the most glaring slop indicators in these kinds of posts.

replies.body: It's already shipped though with 70+ reviews on steam. There are also 20+ threads on the discussion most ignored by the dev and some do touch on the UI. OP basically has all the answers they need already.

replies.body:
It's not unfair, you have many reviews and discussions with no answers from you and 2 people here played it for 10 mins and have given paragraphs of improvements. That tells me your not listening to feedback. It's a fair conclusion is it not?

You don't have to use AI art if comments make you cry, just get some nice asset packs from Itch. Someone posted this earlier [https://itch.io/b/3810/creator-bundle](https://itch.io/b/3810/creator-bundle) "Buy 79 items for **$12**" there is bound to be something in there you can use and there are many more bundles like this. replies.author: Forge450
replies.body: I hear you, some have said the UI is clean/polished and an aspect they enjoyed funny enough people obviously have different opinions. In terms of feedback, since day one I have always been very very open to feedback and my players have actively shaped the game massively since its launch. I simply meant I ignore comments that say "AI slop" blah blah without any thought. That is not feedback as far as I am concerned

replies.author: Forge450
replies.body: To elaborate slightly also it may be you are unfamiliar with the genre? The inspiration was Clicker Heros for example, basically no animations to speak of. The satisfaction/reason to play this Clicker over others is the feel/pacing of the progression and the quality of the content. Most players of the genre care deeply about maths and numbers, many create elaborate spreadsheets for example figuring out the optimal upgrades and the cost and damage scaling curves etc so thats where the game stands out. I spent a lot of time and sleepless nights thinking of and implementing upgrades I genuinely thought were cool or interesting. Granted this perspective would require a deeper look and longer play sessions. But I was only really interested in the design/art aspect for this post but I thought I would explain since you mentioned it :)

replies.author: Forge450
replies.body: Oh and a final peace from my side. You are totally correct from a design and visual perspective I did lean heavily on AI. I am a backend developer. I work behind the scenes and the most important parts to me have always been functionality etc In an ideal world I would have gotten help but the game still doesnt really make anything so its not really possible to do that. Really it was a case of a small solo project that got out of control and became something 10x what I ever expected it would become

comments.author: Officialpolygrafix
comments.body:
Hi, I took a look. (Art director here)   
A couple things:   
1. Yes, there is incongruity in the art direction. You have a kind of futuristic font and UI layout while  you have Kids oriented monster characters. You need to choose a theme and unify against the theme to avoid incongruity.   
2. Before setting theme- Think about who your target audience for playing this is? I get the impression you wanted to make a game for your own kids,  but then decided to release the game for a wider audience so you brought it to steam? It's a fair assumption-  It's an idle clicker game, and quite frankly, i don't know any adults that would sit down on a pc to play an idle clicker game.  It's possible, don't get me wrong, but the audience is probably a very small pool, and thats ok if thats what your going for.. but the question remains - Is the game for children or adults?  This matters because the direction of the art will be guided by this.   
3. Now to answer your question about using AI for art images. I've worked on kids games, and adult games. I can tell you definitively that kids don't have the standard for art that adults do, nor are they negatively impacted by AI that adults are.   So if you choose to use AI art for a kids game, it will be fine, but using ai art for a game that targets adults, you might get some blowback on that because there is a lot of negative sentiment of using AI art out there and i know why.    
Before i get to the reason, just know that i personally don't mind AI. I think theres a place for it, but there is a lot of sensitivity around it because it's displacing artists from work. So a lot of artists that were doing commercial work are either adapting themselves or to a new career.  Especially the graphic artists who's focus was 2d graphics. Chat Gpt is great for businesses and can generate quality work now and no one has to pay a graphic designer $20 - 40 pr hour to do this kind of work, so theres resentment towards ai from a lot of these artists, and thats spilled over into other crowds as well.   
But how it relates is psychology. If your making a kids game for kids- use AI art, it's fine. I probably would have brought it to iphone or android mobile over steam though- its a clicker game. Unify your UI to match the theme of a kids games that has monsters in it.   
IF the game was meant for adults. You've got a lot of things going against it besides the incongruity of the art that you need to consider.   
Not trying to be harsh at all, I want you to succeed in what your doing, but going to point out what i see is going on so you can think about these things.  Hope this helps.

replies.author: Forge450
replies.body:
1. I totally agree with the first point yeah and the theme was generally cartoon/simple little quest adventure style to start but then I liked the font, which is changeable in settings but perhaps changing the default to comic sans as an example would help that initial impression?  
2. Yeah this was something I regret but cant move past at this point. Its not meant for kids at all or in the slightest, its a fairly hardcore numbers/math incremental game I just liked the name since I love alliterated names. I built it because I loved Clicker Heros and couldnt find something that scratched the itch the same way and then friends encouraged me to release it so originally it was for me alone as are most of my projects.  
3. I have always felt like art is a relatively small part of the core experience for the genre. I have played paper clip sim or whatever its called for example that literally is just text and numbers going up no visuals to speak of XD I will also say generally as a person which might be evident by my love of maths and numbers, I have never had much of an appreciation for art, thats just the honest truth  
4. Yeah I understand that perspective totally however there was no universe in which I would have paid an artist for the artwork its just not viable. Either I would have not made the game or I would have made my own terrible looking art, most likely I would have not made it at all or possibly used some existing artists sprites  
5. Again yeah not for kids the idea was a second monitor type of game for pc nerds  
6. I agree and again deeply regret the name. I do think a cute/cartoony style tho doesnt make it solely for kids, adults can enjoy that too.  
7. I appreciate all of the feedback given and a lot of it is spot on and again appreciate the time it took to write all this out so I wanted to respond properly <3

replies.author: Officialpolygrafix
replies.body:
Don't regret making it. Everything we do is a stepping stone towards greater things.   
I didn't realize this wasn't for kids, but thats also my point- It looks like it is, the name implies it is, so i skip it- assuming it is.   
Yes, agreed, adults can enjoy all sorts of graphics. There are games i would never think people would enjoy because of the graphics, but they do. There is an audience out there for everything.  
For AI though.. as i mentioned a lot of adults are sensitive to it. Right now it's artists, and even many programmers. Just join a vibe codeing channel and you'll see. The truth is though AI is coming for their jobs too. So there's resistance, and resentment against it.   
As for art, I think it does a pretty good job on some things, and others not so much, but AI keeps improving, so use it, but i would avoid announcing it unless asked about it.
